headline: An AI wrote a bootable OS kernel from scratch in 38 minutes, passing self-tests
summary: An Anthropic model generated a functional operating-system kernel, capable of booting in an emulator and passing its own tests, in just 38 minutes of compute time. This feat typically requires months of specialized human effort.
details: An Anthropic model successfully built a bootable operating-system kernel from an empty folder in approximately 38 minutes of compute time. This involved around 200 unassisted back-and-forth turns, with the kernel booting inside an emulator and passing its own built-in tests.

Developing a kernel, the innermost core of an operating system that directly interacts with hardware and manages memory, is considered one of the most challenging tasks in software engineering. Such a feat typically demands months of dedicated work from specialist teams.

It's important to note that the model produced a minimal kernel, resembling the core of Windows, rather than a full operating system. While it boots and runs self-checks, it lacks login capabilities or program execution, functioning more as an "engine block" than a complete car.

A notable detail from the write-up reveals that the project had to switch to an older model mid-session. The original model was export-suspended, illustrating the very capabilities that led to its recent shutdown.

The language model achieved this by operating within a tight feedback loop, mimicking a developer's workflow: writing code, attempting compilation, reading errors, fixing them, and repeating the process until the kernel successfully booted and passed tests. Each compilation failure provided crucial information for refinement.

This capability carries significant dual-use implications. The same AI power that can construct complex systems code from scratch could also potentially understand and exploit vulnerabilities in existing systems, a factor contributing to new oversight rules for advanced AI.

However, this achievement represents one documented impressive run by a single developer, and a curated success story doesn't equate to consistent reliability. Details regarding the number of failed attempts, the result's robustness, or its performance on real hardware remain unestablished.
